chapter: Baton Rouge, marriage, learning to play
title: Teaching himself drums and piano; Paul Jacobs
summary: No lessons on drums or piano; learned chords from books, accompanied singing teacher Paul Jacobs, and learned thousands of tunes by ear.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Well, did any musicians help you when you were learning? Yeah.
They played good. And that helped you. That helped me.
Yeah. But they never sat down with a pair of drums and showed you anything?

Not one part of them, no. I wouldn't know of, I don't even know the, what do you call it, parabellum or something? Paradiddle. Diddle, paradiddle. I wouldn't know of paradiddle from a monkey doodle, from a Yankee doodle. Yeah.
And with the piano, did anybody show you chords or anything?
They didn't help you at all? No.
I went and bought the books and taught myself. So you did have some teaching but through books? Through experience and learning.

Yeah. And just got the books, I got chord construction, chord construction and analysis by Gibbs. And I just started from there. And then I had some wonderful experience for five years with Paul Jacobs. Paul Jacobs was nine years in the San Carlos Opera Company. And I played accompaniment for him when he taught singing. Mm-hmm. I had to learn through Paul Jacobs to, to transpose and play in all different keys on the same tune. And I had to drop a half a step by just the sign that he gave me without saying a word. If he, if he turned his finger down and put it right like that, a half an inch, it meant to drop a half a step. Or if he did this, it meant to raise it a half a step. Or if he did that, it meant to raise it one step completely. And then I had to do it without even losing the lead on the melody. That was to suit that particular voice.
Well, so you, but you did pick up reading then of course, that you did that to an extent.
I couldn't read a note. But you, you figured out the chords. But I just, I just listened to thousands of tunes. Yeah, I see. And stayed with the popular hit tunes.
Mm-hmm. I just wondered how you'd pick up the things out of the, out of the book without being able to read. Must have been able to spell, as they say. I said, I know.
He gave me two or three tunes at a time and said, take these home and woodshed them.

And I'd get on and sit on and figure it out and figure it all out. And now if I showed you how I have learned to play the one lead, one line, you understand? Yeah. On mass and all that kind of stuff. I've worked it out to where I can almost sit on and at sight now and read the one line. Mm-hmm. Because I've got thousands and thousands of tunes in the sheet music. Yeah. And I play thousands of tunes because I don't let them leave me by the titles. You understand? I sit down and I may take five different books with titles of tunes. If you wait just a second I'll get one of them and I'll be right back.
